title: Salary Doesn't Mean Exempt: California's Exempt vs. Non-Exempt Traps for Small Employers
author: Brynn Fogerty
excerpt: Understand California’s salary and duties tests, common classification mistakes, and a five-step check for small employers.
cover_alt: an illustration of an HR manager and an employee talking next to a clock
body:
"I pay her a salary, so I don't have to worry about overtime." I hear some version of that sentence almost every month from business owners across Siskiyou County and the Shasta Cascade. It's an understandable assumption-and in California, it's one of the costliest misunderstandings an employer can have.

Last month, we looked at the three biggest traps facing Accidental HR Managers. This month, we're going deeper into the first and most expensive one: classifying employees as exempt or non-exempt.

What "Exempt" Actually Means

An exempt employee is not entitled to overtime pay, and isn't covered by California's meal and rest break rules. A non-exempt employee is-every overtime hour, every meal period, every rest break.

Exempt status is defined by law, not by agreement. You and your employee can't simply decide they're exempt, and paying a salary doesn't make it so. Calling someone a "manager" doesn't either. If the role doesn't meet the legal tests, the employee is non-exempt-regardless of what their offer letter says.

The Two Tests Every Exempt Employee Must Pass

1. The Salary Test

For the most common exemptions (executive, administrative, and professional), California requires a monthly salary of at least twice the state minimum wage for full-time work.

2026 California exempt salary threshold

  • $16.90/hr state minimum wage × 2 × 2,080 hours

  • $70,304 per year minimum

  • $5,858.67 per month · $1,352 per week

This threshold rises whenever the state minimum wage goes up, so a salary that qualified last year may not qualify this year. Some local minimum wages and certain professions (like computer professionals and physicians) have their own, higher thresholds.

2. The Duties Test

This is where most small employers get caught. In California, an exempt employee must be "primarily engaged" in exempt duties-meaning more than 50% of their actual working time. (This is stricter than federal law, which looks at an employee's "primary duty" more loosely.)

Exempt duties generally include:

  • Executive: managing the business or a department, regularly directing two or more full-time employees, and having real input on hiring, firing, and promotions.

  • Administrative: office or non-manual work tied to management policies or business operations, regularly exercising discretion and independent judgment.

  • Professional: licensed or certified professions (law, medicine, accounting, etc.) or work requiring advanced specialized knowledge.

Where Rural Employers Get Caught

In small organizations, people naturally wear many hats. That flexibility is a strength-but it's also what makes classification tricky. Here are the patterns I see most often:

  • The working supervisor. A shop foreman, crew lead, or head cook who manages others but spends most of the day doing the same hands-on work as the team.

  • The "office manager" who mostly does clerical work. Answering phones, filing, data entry, and scheduling are generally non-exempt tasks, even under a management title.

  • The salary that slipped below the line. An employee who was exempt three years ago, but whose pay never caught up with minimum-wage increases.

  • The part-time salaried employee. Prorated salaries often fall below the full-time threshold, which can void the exemption.

What's at Stake

When an employee is misclassified, an employer can be responsible for:

  • Unpaid overtime and double time, going back up to three or four years

  • One hour of premium pay for each missed meal period and each missed rest break

  • Waiting-time penalties of up to 30 days' wages for former employees

  • Wage statement penalties, interest, and attorneys' fees

  • Potential PAGA claims, which can multiply penalties across your workforce

For a small business, a single misclassified role can add up to tens of thousands of dollars. For a rural district or non-profit operating on a tight budget, that's a serious hit-and one that's almost entirely preventable.

A Simple 5-Step Classification Check

  1. List every salaried employee and their current annual pay.

  2. Compare pay to the 2026 threshold ($70,304/year for full-time). Anyone below it is non-exempt.

  3. Track a typical week. Ask each salaried employee to estimate how their time is actually spent.

  4. Apply the 50% rule. If more than half their time goes to non-exempt tasks, they likely need to be reclassified.

  5. Update job descriptions and get guidance on transitioning reclassified employees and addressing any past exposure.

When in doubt, classify as non-exempt

  • Paying hourly with overtime is almost always cheaper than defending a misclassification claim.

  • Reclassifying doesn't have to feel like a demotion-explain it as protecting both of you.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the minimum salary for exempt employees in California in 2026?

$70,304 per year ($1,352 per week), which is twice the 2026 state minimum wage of $16.90 per hour for full-time work.

Can a salaried employee in California be entitled to overtime?

Yes. If a salaried employee doesn't meet both the salary test and the duties test, they are non-exempt and owed overtime and meal and rest breaks.

Is California's duties test different from federal law?

Yes. California requires that exempt employees spend more than 50% of their working time on exempt duties-a stricter, time-based standard than federal law.
